node.label: Cecilia Morgan
node.date_label: Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) · Gendered Pasts, co-edited (1999) · Heroines and History, with Colin M. Coates (2002) · Creating Colonial Pasts (2015) · Commemorating Canada (2016)
node.description: In Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996), Cecilia Morgan argues that gendered language helped constitute political and religious authority in Upper Canada. Masculine public authority and feminine domestic virtue depended on one another, but their meanings and boundaries changed with context. Patrick J. Connor praised the book’s account of class formation while asking for fuller attention to material differences between colony and Britain and to state coercion. Morgan’s “Old Ontario” (2000) proposed connecting feminist history to the workings of a white settler colony, questioning whether Careless’s “limited identities” adequately exposed domination. With Colin M. Coates, Heroines and History (2002) examines the commemoration of Madeleine de Verchères and Laura Secord. Her later work follows the making and transmission of historical memory. Reviewing Commemorating Canada (2016), Harold Kalman welcomed its accessible overview while questioning its account of the mandates of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board and Parks Canada.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Public Men and Virtuous Women: The Gendered Languages of Religion and Politics in Upper Canada, 1791–1850 (1996); Gendered Pasts: Historical Essays in Femininity and Masculinity in Canada (1999, co-edited with Kathryn McPherson and Nancy M. Forestell; UTP reprint 2003); “Old Ontario” Through the Lens of Feminist Scholarship, 1970s–1990s (2000); Heroines and History: Representations of Madeleine de Verchères and Laura Secord (2002, with Colin M. Coates); “Making Heroes, Selling Heritage” (2010); Creating Colonial Pasts: History, Memory, and Commemoration in Southern Ontario, 1860–1980 (2015); Commemorating Canada: History, Heritage, and Memory, 1850s–1990s (2016); Travellers through Empire: Indigenous Voyages from Early Canada (2017).
node.scope_note: Read: Morgan’s “Old Ontario” PDF pp. 1–9, with selected notes and bibliography; “Making Heroes, Selling Heritage” (2010), paragraphs 1–23 and notes; Connor’s 1997 review; selected substantive paragraphs of Kalman’s 2018 review; selected Bradbury passages in Paré’s authorized 2023 translation of the 2008 chapter. Public Men and Virtuous Women is known here through its publisher and Connor; Heroines and History through metadata and displayed chapter openings; the 2015–2017 monographs through publisher, catalogue or reviewer evidence. No complete monograph read. The Scott, Anderson and Habermas links are Connor’s reported attributions, with particular source works unspecified. The original English Bradbury chapter, inaccessible journal passages and full Toronto profile remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Connor’s 1997 review reads Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) as extending Scott’s relational analysis of gender.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Connor, PDF p. 1, opening paragraph, explicitly names Scott and cites Morgan p. 9. A named reader's attribution; Morgan's introduction and the particular Scott text remain unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Scott’s gender analysis, as Connor reads Morgan

proposed_edges.relationship: Connor (1997) attributes Morgan’s imagined middle-class community in Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) partly to Anderson.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Connor, PDF p. 4, first paragraph, citing Morgan pp. 19–20. He names Anderson and Habermas together; their separate shares and particular works are unspecified. Book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Connor (1997) also identifies Habermas as a resource for Public Men and Virtuous Women’s (1996) account of class community.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Same explicit joint attribution, Connor PDF p. 4, first paragraph. This is a reported resource, with no particular Habermas title or independently verified direct debt asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Old Ontario” (2000), Morgan finds Careless’s “limited identities” insufficiently attentive to domination and resistance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary PDF p. 8, paragraph beginning If anything, with n. 16 identifying Careless's 1969 essay. She calls the concept ‘fairly benign’ and proposes an additional settler-colony frame. The cited Careless essay itself was not newly read; this is her qualified assessment, not wholesale rejection.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions the power analysis in “limited identities”

proposed_edges.relationship: Morgan’s “Making Heroes, Selling Heritage” (2010) praises McKay and Bates’s In the Province of History (2010) while questioning its omission of school textbooks.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary review, para. 21: ‘school textbooks and readers’; paras. 22–23 retain praise and contextual comparison. Robin Bates shares the book's argument but lacks an eligible endpoint; no sole McKay authorship implied. Book unread independently.
proposed_edges.map_label: McKay and Bates: school readers omitted

proposed_edges.relationship: Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) interprets gendered public and domestic authority as unstable, interconnected constructions in Upper Canada.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UTP description, final two paragraphs: gender meanings varied by context and boundaries repeatedly failed. Publisher synopsis only for this book claim; Morgan's 2000 essay provides a separately read historiographical intervention.

proposed_edges.relationship: Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996) treats Upper Canadian Methodism, attacked by the colonial elite, as a religious arena where ideas of gender, race and class interacted with politics.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UTP description, paragraphs on evangelical discourse and religion/politics in the 1840s. Connor's review pp. 2–3 was also read. This concerns gender and religious authority, not an asserted position in the later secularization debate.
proposed_edges.map_label: Gender in religion and colonial politics

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Making Heroes, Selling Heritage” (2010), Morgan asks memory historians to connect reception, classroom transmission and individual choices about commemoration.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary review, paras. 21–23. Her school-textbook objection and closing emphasis on choices about remembrance supply the claim. Reviewing two monographs does not establish a complete theory of collective memory or the founding of the field.
proposed_edges.map_label: Reception, schooling and individual choices in memory

proposed_edges.relationship: “Old Ontario” (2000) proposes studying Ontario as a white settler colony, connecting gendered power to national and imperial processes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary PDF pp. 8–9, concluding paragraphs after the Careless discussion. The proposal extends analysis beyond conventional colonial institutions while preserving differences among colonies. No adoption of Wolfe's theory or membership in a later school is inferred; no community knowledge is reproduced.
proposed_edges.map_label: A settler-colony frame for Ontario feminist history

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Cecilia Morgan’s Travellers through Empire (2017), J. R. Miller (2018) argues that its emphasis on gender and racial identity underestimates the practical purposes of many of the people whose journeys it examines.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Miller’s review on pp. 122–124, distinguishing its beginning from the preceding review on p. 122. Miller praises the research and analysis but disputes the relative emphasis placed on identity and practical purposes. This edge records his qualified criticism, not an unqualified rejection. Morgan’s book was not read. The claim concerns published historical interpretation only; no community knowledge or biographical details of the book’s subjects are reproduced.
proposed_edges.map_label: Questions the weighting of gender, identity and practical purposes

proposed_edges.relationship: In Heroines and History (2002), coauthored with Colin M. Coates, Cecilia Morgan contributes to Canadian cultural history through literary analysis of historical narratives about Laura Secord, a method Renée Hulan’s 2005 review essay identifies as productive cooperation between literary criticism and historical research.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Hulan’s journal-hosted essay, particularly its sustained discussion of Heroines and History in paragraphs 16–19. Paragraph 16 distinguishes Morgan’s narrative analysis from Coates’s section; paragraph 19 discusses historical difference and the contextual interpretation of commemorative writing. The mapping to English-Canadian intellectual and cultural history is editorial and limited to this named methodological contribution. Hulan has no eligible person endpoint, so no person-to-person edge is proposed. The coauthored book itself was not read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Literary analysis of Canadian historical narratives

proposed_edges.relationship: Cecilia Morgan’s Commemorating Canada (2016) provides an account of labour’s marginal place in public commemoration and a warning against celebratory simplification that Janis Thiessen applies in “Remembering 1919: The Winnipeg General Strike” (2020).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s HTML research note, with particular attention to the introductory framing, concluding discussion and notes 17–19 and 56. Thiessen uses Morgan in the body to contextualize labour commemoration and to qualify celebratory accounts of the strike. Notes 18–19 identify Commemorating Canada, pp. 102 and 164; note 56 identifies p. 184. The edge records a specific resource used within Canadian working-class history. Thiessen has no eligible person endpoint, so no person-to-person edge is proposed. Morgan’s book was not read. No interview quotations or family histories are reproduced.
proposed_edges.map_label: A resource for analysing labour commemoration
